slides.text: Sorted array + pair sum → opposite ends: l at the front, r at the back; too small moves l in, too big moves r in.
slides.alt: Under "Sorted array, pair / triplet sum → Opposite ends", Python two_sum(numbers, target) with l, r = 0, len(numbers) - 1 and while l < r; the branch if s < target: l += 1 is highlighted with the note "Sum too small: move l in". On 2, 7, 11, 15, l is on 2 and r on 7: 2 + 7 = 9.

slides.text: Remove / move while reading ahead → fast & slow: fast explores, slow marks the end of what you keep.
slides.alt: Under "Remove / move while reading ahead → Fast / slow", Python remove_duplicates(nums) with if nums[fast] != nums[slow]: slow += 1; nums[slow] = nums[fast] highlighted and the note "Something new? slow steps forward, takes it". The array reads 0, 1, 2, 3 kept, then dimmed values, with fast on a 4: 4 is new.

slides.text: Area between two lines → move inward, always the shorter side (the taller one can never raise the minimum).
slides.alt: Under "Container / area between indices → Inward from tallest hope", Python max_area(h) with if h[l] < h[r]: l += 1 else: r -= 1 highlighted and the note "Move the shorter side: the taller one can never raise the minimum". Heights 1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7; returns 49.

slides.text: Merge two sorted lists → one pointer each: take the smaller head, then append the rest.
slides.alt: Under "Merge two sorted streams → One pointer each", Python merge(a, b) with return out + a[i:] + b[j:] highlighted and the note "One runs out: append the rest". a is 1, 2, 4 and b is 1, 3, 4: + the rest → [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4].

slides.text: Watch l < r: with l <= r the middle element can pair with itself.
slides.alt: "Two traps": forgetting the sort prerequisite (opposite-end sum logic is wrong on unsorted data; sort first or pick another pattern) and crossing pointers (the loop condition is usually l < r; equality can double-count the middle element). while l < r ✓ against while l <= r, where [3], 6 → [1, 1] ✗.
